title: 59. Numeracy & Number Systems: Multiplying and Dividing Radicals
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Multiply two square roots using the product rule for radicals.
questions.question: Simplify \(\sqrt{3}\cdot\sqrt{5}\).
questions.explanation: For nonnegative radicands, use the product rule for square roots: \(\sqrt{a}\cdot\sqrt{b}=\sqrt{ab}\). Therefore, \(\sqrt{3}\cdot\sqrt{5}=\sqrt{15}\). The alternative adds radicands even though the radicals are being multiplied.
questions.hint: Multiply the numbers under the radical signs.

questions.learningObjective: Multiply square roots and simplify the resulting perfect square.
questions.question: Simplify \(\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{8}\).
questions.explanation: By the product rule, \(\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{16}\). Since \(4^2=16\), \(\sqrt{16}=4\). The alternative stops at the radicand without taking its square root.
questions.hint: Multiply the radicands first, then simplify the square root.

questions.learningObjective: Simplify a product of square roots by extracting a perfect square factor.
questions.question: Simplify \(\sqrt{6}\cdot\sqrt{10}\).
questions.explanation: Use the product rule: \(\sqrt{6}\cdot\sqrt{10}=\sqrt{60}\). Since \(60=4\cdot15\), \(\sqrt{60}=\sqrt{4}\sqrt{15}=2\sqrt{15}\). The alternative extracts the square factor itself rather than its square root.
questions.hint: Multiply the radicands and look for a perfect square factor.

questions.learningObjective: Divide two square roots using the quotient rule for radicals.
questions.question: Simplify \(\frac{\sqrt{48}}{\sqrt{3}}\).
questions.explanation: For a nonnegative numerator radicand and a positive denominator radicand, use the quotient rule for square roots: \(\frac{\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{b}}=\sqrt{\frac{a}{b}}\). Thus \(\frac{\sqrt{48}}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{\frac{48}{3}}=\sqrt{16}=4\). The alternative does not have square equal to the radicand quotient.
questions.hint: Divide the numbers under the radical signs before simplifying.

questions.learningObjective: Simplify a quotient of square roots with a perfect square result.
questions.question: Simplify \(\frac{\sqrt{50}}{\sqrt{2}}\).
questions.explanation: Apply the quotient rule: \(\frac{\sqrt{50}}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{50}{2}}=\sqrt{25}=5\). The alternative \(10\) comes from multiplying the radicands instead of dividing them: \(\sqrt{50\cdot2}=\sqrt{100}=10\).
questions.hint: Use the quotient rule and then take the square root.

questions.concept: Multiplying Square Roots with Perfect Square Products
questions.learningObjective: Simplify a product of square roots that results in a perfect square.
questions.question: Simplify \(\sqrt{12}\cdot\sqrt{3}\).
questions.explanation: Using the product rule, \(\sqrt{12}\cdot\sqrt{3}=\sqrt{36}\). Since \(6^2=36\), \(\sqrt{36}=6\). The alternative has square unequal to the radicand product.
questions.hint: Multiply the radicands and simplify the resulting square root.

questions.learningObjective: Simplify a quotient of square roots by dividing the radicands.
questions.question: Simplify \(\frac{\sqrt{72}}{\sqrt{8}}\).
questions.explanation: Apply the quotient rule: \(\frac{\sqrt{72}}{\sqrt{8}}=\sqrt{\frac{72}{8}}=\sqrt{9}=3\). The alternative \(6\) comes from writing \(\sqrt{72}=6\sqrt{2}\) and \(\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}\), canceling \(\sqrt{2}\), and then forgetting to divide by the remaining coefficient \(2\).
questions.hint: Divide the radicands first, then evaluate the square root.

questions.concept: Multiplying Square Roots with Large Products
questions.learningObjective: Simplify a product of square roots by evaluating the resulting perfect square.
questions.question: Simplify \(\sqrt{5}\cdot\sqrt{20}\).
questions.explanation: Use the product rule: \(\sqrt{5}\cdot\sqrt{20}=\sqrt{100}\). Since \(10^2=100\), \(\sqrt{100}=10\). The alternative inserts an extra radical factor.
questions.hint: Multiply the numbers under the radicals and simplify.

questions.concept: Combining Multiplication and Division of Radicals
questions.learningObjective: Simplify an expression involving both multiplication and division of square roots.
questions.question: Simplify \(\frac{\sqrt{24}\cdot\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{2}}\).
questions.explanation: Combine the radicands into a single square root: \(\frac{\sqrt{24}\cdot\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{24\cdot6}{2}}=\sqrt{72}\). Since \(72=36\cdot2\), \(\sqrt{72}=\sqrt{36}\sqrt{2}=6\sqrt{2}\). The alternative loses a factor of two in the rationalized denominator.
questions.hint: Combine all radicands into one radical before simplifying.

questions.learningObjective: Simplify a radical expression that combines multiplication and division in one step.
questions.question: Simplify \(\frac{\sqrt{27}\cdot\sqrt{8}}{\sqrt{6}}\).
questions.explanation: Combine the radicands: \(\frac{\sqrt{27}\cdot\sqrt{8}}{\sqrt{6}}=\sqrt{\frac{27\cdot8}{6}}=\sqrt{\frac{216}{6}}=\sqrt{36}=6\). The alternative retains a radical after the radicands have canceled to a perfect square.
questions.hint: Write the entire expression as a single square root, then simplify the fraction under the radical.
